title: Rowan and the Loud Duck Horn
markdown:
The Great Library Quiz Night of Oakhaven was a serious affair — not archive-serious, but the high-stakes serious of people armed with answers and a year’s bragging rights. Rowan the pine marten, happiest with oil-stained paws and blueprints for brake pads, had come only because Aunt Mabel insisted. Mabel was a distinguished owl who could predict the flight paths of birds no one else had heard of, and she believed quizzes were good for the soul.

“Keeps the mind nimble,” she had hooted, golden eyes like polished brass. “And they’re serving Mrs. Gable’s legendary treacle tarts.”

Rowan’s whiskers, usually as precise as a mechanic on a loose bolt, quivered. He hated the centre of a room. Give him the click of a well-oiled chain, a job done right and unheralded. His workshop behind the old mill hummed with oil, rubber, and worn metal. Tonight Mrs. Higgins, the librarian whose spectacles magnified sternness to dinner-plate size, had added an interactive element.

“For our final, thrilling segment! A Wheel of Fortune of Oakhaven’s most interesting professions. When it lands on your category, you step forward and answer for your trade.”

Rowan’s stomach somersaulted like a chain snapping mid-hill. He tried to sink into velvet, wishing for his dullest tweed. Mabel’s nudge was a falling feather and still reached him. “Don’t fret. You are not only Rowan the mechanic. You are Rowan, master of two-wheeled wonders.”

The wheel whirred like a thousand bees. It teetered between two dreadful labels and thunked on Local Craftsmen & Mechanics. Mrs. Higgins’s finger found him like a compass. “Rowan! Our bicycle virtuoso. Come up.”

He wanted to dissolve into the periodicals. Oakhaven’s eyes would not allow it. Mabel’s push was gentle and absolute. “Courage. We are not in trouble. We are merely visible. And visibility, sometimes, lets us be helpful.”

He shuffled. The prop waited on a side table, forlorn until named. It was an oversized antique bicycle horn shaped, with surprising devotion, like a duck’s head. The beak hung slightly ajar, mid-quack. Cool ceramic, a faint smell of cellar dust and old rubber bulb, a weight that sat in the paws like a sleeping animal. Its painted eyes held an impish wet gleam, as if the thing had been listening to the quiz all evening and taking notes.

Mrs. Higgins lifted it. For a breath it seemed to possess a will. “Do not ask it to speak,” she said, half joke, half house rule, “unless the library itself is in need. It is decorative. Entirely.”

That was the condition. Rowan accepted the horn as one accepts a sleeping cat: carefully, and without questions.

Her elbow brushed a stack of very old, very tall encyclopedias. Bindings worn, pages brittle, they began to topple — a silent avalanche of knowledge. A pine marten who wished to vanish still reached for the pages. Kindness to the books came first. His paw knocked the duck.

It spoke.

Not a toot. Not a polite honk. A deep, resonant, earth-shattering QUACK that drowned the gasp and the clatter. The taboo lay in pieces on the carpet with Volume M.

Stunned hush. Then muffled laughter, snickers widening into chuckles. Rowan’s fur prickled. This was the attention he had built a workshop to avoid. He clutched the horn. It seemed to smirk. The companion, if it was a companion, had been separated from its silence; he from his hiding.

Mabel, in the seats, offered a soft amused hoot and did not come to take the thing away. She knew he was a fixer.

He looked at the ceramic beak, took the quiet after the storm, and did not run. The room could still be kind if he was. “Ah. Yes.” He held the Grand Quacker up, voice rusty, then finding gravel enough. “A rare find. Unparalleled acoustic projection. For emergencies. If the library were on fire, a gentle toot would not suffice. This is for situations requiring immediate, undeniable attention.”

The explanation was a kindness to the object and to the listeners who might otherwise have made him only a joke. The horn’s smirk softened, or he imagined it did.

Mr. Abernathy, the notoriously punctilious mayor, leaned forward to note the falling encyclopedias. Rowan timed a second QUACK not as revenge but as a shared startle — an invitation into the absurdity rather than a spotlight left only on himself. Spectacles jumped. Titters rose, warmer. Abernathy, after a moment, actually smiled, which in Oakhaven counted as weather.

The horn changed in that breath. The impish gleam went ordinary and bright; the cellar-dust smell became simply old rubber; the duck’s head, which had seemed to watch, became a tool that had chosen usefulness over décor. No feathers, no flesh — only the true form of a thing that had wanted, all along, to be used.

Later, quiz done, they sat on the cool library steps. Villagers drifted past with the last of the tart crumbs and the ordinary gossip of who had known the cobblestone count. Through the arched greenhouse roof the sky went indigo, the colour of old ink. Damp earth and night-blooming jasmine. Rowan turned the horn in his paws, souvenir now, still faintly warm from the second quack. In the workshop it would live beside the brake-pad blueprints, a ridiculous neighbour to sensible metal.

“You handled that rather well,” Mabel said, blanket-warm. “Impeccable comic timing. Almost theatrical.”

He chuckled, a rumble that surprised him. He had been so busy avoiding being seen that he had not considered that visibility could help — catch books, wake a mayor, make a hall laugh without malice. The useful kind of being noticed, even loud, sat better than the decorative kind of hiding.

Mabel’s eyes held the twilight. She did not need to gild it. Rowan looked back at the library’s window-glow. He would still prefer gears and chains. He also, traitorously, looked forward to the next quiz, the horn on his workshop shelf, ready for a well-timed QUACK. That warmth outdid even Mrs. Gable’s tarts. The duck, no longer a beast, kept its beak ajar as if mid-laugh, and Rowan, loyal to the aunt who had made him visible, carried it home like a promise he intended to keep.
characters: Rowan (a pine marten bike mechanic), Mabel (an owl aunt)
